title: What Is Retro Pay? A Small Business Guide
summary: What is retro pay? It’s the gap between what an employee was paid and what they earned. Learn how to calculate it, tax it, and pay it on time, step by step
body_markdown:
A raise gets approved on the 1st. Payroll doesn’t pick it up until three pay periods later. Now your employee is owed the difference, and the next paycheck will carry a line item that says “retro.”


So, what is retro pay? It’s the money you owe to correct a past paycheck that came up short. This guide covers how to calculate it, how it’s taxed, and when you have to pay it. If you’re an employee staring at an unfamiliar pay stub line, we cover that too.


## **What Is Retro Pay? The Short Answer and What You Owe**


Retro pay, short for retroactive pay, is the money an employer owes to correct a past paycheck that came up short. You calculate the gap between what the employee earned and what they received, then pay it on the next paycheck or as a separate payment.


- **When you owe it:** An employee was underpaid by a missed raise, wrong rate, or miscalculated overtime.
- **How it’s paid:** Next paycheck or a separate payment.
- **How it’s taxed:** Retro pay is generally taxable wages. Federal income tax withholding may follow the IRS supplemental wage rules.
- **When it’s due:** Minimum wage and overtime are due on the regular payday. Overtime you can’t calculate in time is due by the next payday after you can.


## **How Does Retro Pay Work?**


Retro pay works as a correction. You find the gap between what an employee earned and what they received, calculate the gross difference, and add it to the next paycheck or issue it separately. Label it clearly on the pay stub and withhold taxes as you would on regular wages.


Here’s the process from start to finish:


1. Confirm the error and the pay periods it affected.
2. Calculate the gross difference between what was owed and what was paid.
3. Add it to the next paycheck, or run a separate payment.
4. Label it as retro pay on the pay stub, with the pay periods covered where possible.
5. Withhold taxes the way you would on regular wages.
6. Keep a record of the error, the fix, and the payment date.


Retro pay covers pay an employee is owed for a past period, so treat it like any other payroll item. A short note to the employee before the corrected check arrives goes a long way.


## **When Do Employers Owe Retro Pay?**


Most retro pay situations come from manual steps, not carelessness. A rate doesn’t update, a number gets keyed wrong, or a shift type gets miscoded. Here are the most common causes:


- **Late or missed raises.** A raise was approved but didn’t reach payroll before the next run. This is the top cause of retro pay on[raises for hourly employees](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/employee-raises-hourly-employees) .
- **Miscalculated overtime.** A covered, nonexempt employee worked more than 40 hours in a workweek but was paid the regular rate instead of time-and-a-half. Read the[federal overtime rules](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fact-sheets/23-flsa-overtime-pay) , and review the[overtime laws by state](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/overtime-laws-by-state) , since requirements differ by location.
- **Wrong shift differential.** A night or holiday shift should have paid a higher rate, but the[shift differential](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/shift-differential) wasn’t applied.
- **Missed or delayed commissions.** A commission was earned but not paid on time.
- **Minimum wage increases.** A new minimum wage took effect, but payroll still used the old rate.
- **Retroactive raises and contract changes.** A new agreement applies to a past effective date.
- **Data entry and processing errors.** A typo or a system mismatch put the wrong number on the check. Learn more about common[payroll errors](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/payroll-errors) .


One distinction matters. Employers must pay wages employees have already earned, including applicable minimum wage and overtime. Whether an employer must honor a retroactive raise depends on the applicable law and the terms of the compensation agreement, policy, or other commitment.


Primo Stropoli, owner of Tetta’s Market, describes the old way of doing things: “I was actually manually calculating if someone clocked in at 8:01 and worked until 3:15.” Math like that is where errors hide.


When an employee flags a[payroll error](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/payroll-correction) , move fast. Cambria Wallace, a certified payroll professional on the Homebase payroll team, puts it this way: “Employers should investigate and have a plan in place on how to fix issues, rectified by the next payroll.”


If your team flags errors often, look at your process. Homebase[payroll](https://www.joinhomebase.com/payroll) turns approved timesheets directly into payroll data, so no one retypes hours by hand.


## **What’s the Difference Between Retro Pay and Back Pay?**


People use the two terms interchangeably, and sources draw the line in different places. In practice:


- **Retro pay** commonly refers to a payroll correction for an earlier period. The usual cause is a missed raise, a wrong rate, or an unapplied differential.
- **Back pay** is compensation owed for work already performed but not properly paid. The U.S. Department of Labor (DOL) also uses “back pay” for the recovery of wages after a violation.


Check which term your payroll app uses on the pay stub. The label matters less than the fix, because both need to be paid correctly.


Under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), employees generally have two years to bring a claim for unpaid minimum wage or overtime. That extends to three years for willful violations. Qualifying claims may also include liquidated damages equal to the unpaid wages, according to the[DOL](https://www.dol.gov/general/topic/wages/backpay) . A prompt fix keeps a small error small.


## **What Does Retro Pay Look Like on a Pay Stub?**


If you spotted an unfamiliar line item on your paycheck, this section is for you. If you’re an employer, it helps you explain the line to your team.


Retro pay on a paycheck usually appears as its own line item. The label depends on your payroll app:


- **Retro pay or retro earnings:** A general label for any retroactive wage correction.
- **Retro regular or retro regular pay:** Regular hours that were underpaid in an earlier period.
- **Retro OT or retro overtime:** Overtime hours paid at the wrong rate.
- **Retro adjustment:** A catch-all label some apps use for any correction.


A clear pay statement should identify the correction and, where possible, the pay periods it covers.


### **What Is Retro Regular Pay on a Pay Stub?**


Retro regular pay means your regular hours were underpaid in an earlier period. The most common cause is a raise that didn’t apply on time. If you should have earned $18 an hour but were paid $16 for two weeks, the $2 difference on every hour shows up as retro regular pay on your next check.


### **What Is Retro Overtime Pay on a Pay Stub?**


Retro overtime pay means your overtime hours were paid at the wrong rate. Say you worked 45 hours in a week but were paid your regular rate for all 45. The missing premium on the last five hours shows up as retro overtime on your next paycheck.


Seeing either line isn’t a red flag. It means your employer caught the error and corrected it.


## **How to Calculate Retro Pay**


The formula is simple: **retro pay = correct amount owed minus amount already paid.** Calculate it on gross pay, before taxes. Then withhold taxes as you would on any paycheck.


### **Retro Pay Example: Hourly Employee**


Mia earns $15 an hour. Last week, she worked 50 hours: 40 regular hours and 10 overtime hours. Payroll paid her $15 for all 50 hours, including the overtime hours, but failed to add the required overtime premium.


- **What she was paid:** $15 × 50 hours = $750.
- **What she should have been paid:** (40 × $15) + (10 × $22.50) = $825.
- **Retro pay owed:** $825 minus $750 = $75.


Because Mia already received straight-time pay for all 50 hours, the correction is the missing half-time premium on her 10 overtime hours. That’s $7.50 for each overtime hour.


### **Retro Pay Example: Salaried Employee**


Jamil earns $50,000 a year, paid biweekly. A $3,000 raise brings his salary to $53,000, but the raise misses his first paycheck.


- **Old gross pay per period:** $50,000 ÷ 26 = $1,923.08.
- **New gross pay per period:** $53,000 ÷ 26 = $2,038.46.
- **Retro pay owed:** $2,038.46 minus $1,923.08 = $115.38.


His next paycheck should include his regular pay of $2,038.46 plus the $115.38 in retro pay, for a total of $2,153.84.


### **Retro Pay Example: Raise Missed for Several Pay Periods**


A raise from $16 to $18 an hour takes effect on the 1st, but payroll doesn’t apply it for three biweekly pay periods. The employee worked 80 hours in each period.


- **Difference per hour:** $18 minus $16 = $2.
- **Retro pay owed:** $2 × 80 hours × three periods = $480.


If the employee also worked overtime in those periods, recalculate the overtime at the new rate. Bonuses and other pay that count toward the regular rate can change that math. To verify the hours first, use our[free time card calculator](https://www.joinhomebase.com/free-time-card-calculator) .


## **Is Retro Pay Taxed Higher?**


No. Retro pay is taxable wages, and the rate doesn’t go up because it’s a correction. Federal income tax, Social Security, Medicare, and any state and local taxes apply. The confusion comes from how it’s withheld, since a large payout can look like heavier withholding in a single paycheck.


The IRS lists retroactive pay increases and back pay as supplemental wages. That gives you two ways to withhold federal income tax.


### **Percentage Method (Flat Rate)**


You can withhold a flat 22% for federal income tax on eligible supplemental wages up to $1 million. This works when you identify the retro pay separately from regular wages, and you withheld federal income tax from the employee’s regular wages this year or last. It’s the simpler option for a separate payment. Supplemental wages over $1 million paid to an employee in a calendar year are withheld at 37%.


### **Aggregate Method**


Combine the retro pay with the employee’s regular wages and calculate withholding on the combined total. Then subtract the tax already withheld on the regular wages. This takes more work, and it’s the method to use when the flat-rate conditions aren’t met. The details are in[IRS Publication 15](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p15) .


The 22% is a withholding rate, not the employee’s final tax rate. For 2026, Social Security withholding is 6.2% up to the $184,500 wage base, and Medicare withholding is 1.45% with no wage cap. You also owe a matching employer share of both. Employers must withhold an additional 0.9% in Medicare tax from an employee’s wages above $200,000 in a calendar year. That Additional Medicare Tax is an employee tax, not a matching employer tax. For more on how it all fits together, read our guide to[payroll tax withholding](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/payroll-tax-withholding) .


If you correct pay from a prior calendar year, review your wage reporting. Depending on the facts, you may need to adjust tax documents. When in doubt, run it through your payroll system rather than calculating by hand. Cambria Wallace recommends that you “contact Payroll Support if you’re unsure how to fix the issue or if a payment needs to be voided and re-run to ensure the correct taxes are withheld.”


## **How Long Does an Employer Have to Pay Retro Pay?**


The Fair Labor Standards Act sets no fixed number of days. The Department of Labor expects minimum wage and overtime on the regular payday. If you can’t calculate overtime in time, pay it as soon as practicable, and no later than the next payday after you can. State laws can be stricter.


That standard comes from the DOL’s[Field Operations Handbook](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/field-operations-handbook/Chapter-30) , and the delayed-calculation fallback addresses overtime specifically. For other retro pay, like a retroactive raise, there’s no single federal deadline. Your state’s payday rules apply, and the safest move is to pay on the next paycheck once the amount is confirmed.


State rules vary, so check your state labor department for current deadlines. The DOL’s[state payday requirements](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/state/payday) page is a starting point, and our[state labor law guides](https://www.joinhomebase.com/state-labor-laws) can help. You can also read how the[FLSA](https://www.joinhomebase.com/hr-compliance/flsa) applies to your business. Late payment of wages can lead to wage claims, so don’t wait on a deadline.


As soon as you know about the error, start the clock. If waiting for your next scheduled payroll would run past the deadline, run an off-cycle payroll instead. Homebase includes unlimited payroll runs for one monthly fee, so an off-cycle correction doesn’t add a per-run charge.


## **How to Avoid Retro Pay Mistakes**


The best retro pay situation is the one you never have to handle. Four habits help.


**Apply raises right away.** The moment you approve a raise, update the rate in your payroll app. Most retro pay on raises happens because the change slipped by one pay period.


**Track overtime automatically.** Manual overtime math is where errors hide. Homebase calculates hours, breaks, and overtime from your team’s time clock, and sends overtime alerts before someone crosses the threshold. Cherie Chua, co-founder of Luxe Bites, says: “It’s just so clear-cut to see the breakdown, and if you ever have to edit it, you just unlock the time sheet.”


**Add a pre-payroll review.** Before each payroll run, check total hours, rate changes, and anyone who worked a different shift type. Have managers approve timecards first, and use the timesheet edit history to see who changed what. Riley McGuire, director of HR at Student Agencies, compares each person’s hours to the prior period: “...if someone worked like 10 hours the last pay period and suddenly is working like 50 hours, that’s something to be alarmed by and go back and check.” Catching a mistake before payroll runs is a five-minute fix.


**Keep time tracking and payroll in one app.** When hours live in one place and payroll lives in another, someone has to move the numbers by hand. Putting[time tracking](https://www.joinhomebase.com/time-clock/time-tracking) and payroll together removes that handoff. Our Payroll Assistant also flags issues before payday.


## **Frequently Asked Questions About Retro Pay**


### **How Does Retro Pay Work?**


### **Is Retro Pay a Raise?**


Retro pay is not a raise, but a raise can create it. If a raise takes effect on one date and payroll applies it later, the employee is owed the difference for the gap. The retro payment covers that missed pay, and the new rate applies going forward.


### **How Much Retro Pay Will I Get?**


The amount is the correct pay minus the pay already received. For hourly employees, multiply the rate difference by the hours affected. For salaried employees, find the per-period difference and multiply it by the number of periods. Taxes come out of that gross figure, so take-home pay is lower.


### **What’s the Difference Between Retro Pay and Back Pay?**


Retro pay commonly refers to a payroll correction for an earlier period, usually from a missed raise or rate. Back pay is compensation owed for work performed but not properly paid, and the Department of Labor uses it for wages recovered after a violation. Sources draw the line differently, so check which term your payroll system uses.


### **Is Retro Pay Taxed Higher?**


No. Retro pay may qualify as supplemental wages, so federal income tax, Social Security, and Medicare apply. When IRS conditions are met, withholding can use the flat 22% rate on separately identified pay, or the aggregate method. A large payout can look like heavier withholding in one paycheck, not a higher tax rate.


### **Is Retro Pay Legally Required?**


Yes, when the pay was already earned. Unpaid minimum wage or overtime must be paid, and employees may also recover an equal amount in liquidated damages in qualifying claims under the Fair Labor Standards Act. Whether you must honor a retroactive raise depends on applicable law and the terms of your compensation agreement or policy.


### **How Long Does an Employer Have to Pay Retro Pay?**


The Fair Labor Standards Act sets no fixed number of days. The Department of Labor expects minimum wage and overtime on the regular payday. If overtime can’t be calculated in time, pay it as soon as practicable, and no later than the next payday after you can compute it. State laws can be stricter.


### **How Far Back Can Retro Pay Go?**


Under the Fair Labor Standards Act, employees generally have two years to bring a claim for unpaid minimum wage or overtime, and three years if the violation was willful. State limits can differ. A retroactive raise can reach back to whatever effective date the employer, contract, or agreement set.


## **Stop Correcting Paychecks. Start Preventing the Problem.**


Retro pay is a correction. It’s pay your employee is owed for a past period. Minimum wage and overtime generally must be paid on the applicable regular payday. If overtime can’t be calculated in time, the Department of Labor’s guidance says to pay it as soon as practicable, and no later than the next payday after it can be calculated. State law may add requirements.
